use: 'Fuzakenaide' means 'Stop messing around'; 'Fuzakeru na!' is an angry 'Don't screw with me!'.

example.ja: ふざけないで、ちゃんと聞いてよ。
example.english: Stop messing around and listen properly.

examplePolite.ja: ふざけないで、ちゃんと聞いてください。
examplePolite.english: Please stop messing around and listen properly.

notes: Fuzaketa describes something outrageous: 'fuzaketa hanashi' (a ridiculous story).

english: be funny, get a laugh; go down well
use: 'Ukeru!' alone is a casual 'LOL, that's hilarious'.

example.romaji: Kare no joudan, minna ni uketeta ne.
example.ja: 彼の冗談、みんなにウケてたね。

examplePolite.romaji: Kare no joudan, minna ni ukete imashita ne.
examplePolite.ja: 彼の冗談、みんなにウケていましたね。

notes: Also a product or idea catching on: 'Wakai hito ni ukete iru'.

use: Said of something funny: 'Kore, maji waraeru'. Also 'Ima nara waraeru' (I can laugh about it now).

examplePolite.romaji: Kono douga, hontou ni waraemasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: この動画、本当に笑えますよ。

example.ja: もう、そんなにからかわないでよ。
example.english: Come on, stop teasing me like that.

examplePolite.ja: そんなにからかわないでくださいよ。
examplePolite.english: Please stop teasing me like that.

notes: Lighter than baka ni suru (make fun of, look down on).

english: liven up, get lively; get excited (as a group)
use: For parties, chats or crowds getting fun.

example.romaji: Kinou no nomikai, sugoku moriagatta ne.
example.ja: 昨日の飲み会、すごく盛り上がったね。
example.english: Last night's drinks were really lively, weren't they?

examplePolite.romaji: Kinou no nomikai wa sugoku moriagarimashita ne.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日の飲み会はすごく盛り上がりましたね。
examplePolite.english: Last night's drinks were really lively, weren't they?

notes: Moriageru is making it lively: 'ba o moriageru' (liven up the room).

use: For films, music, kindness or a view that stirs you: 'Kandou shita!'.

example.romaji: Ano eiga, hontou ni kandou shita.
example.ja: あの映画、本当に感動した。

examplePolite.romaji: Ano eiga ni wa hontou ni kandou shimashita.
examplePolite.ja: あの映画には本当に感動しました。

notes: Wider than English 'moved': also for being blown away by great food or skill.

use: For one person's excitement or agitation.

example.ja: 興奮して全然寝れなかった。
example.english: I was too excited to sleep at all.

examplePolite.ja: 興奮して全然眠れませんでした。
examplePolite.english: I was too excited to sleep at all.

notes: It can also mean agitated or angry, so wakuwaku suru is safer for happy anticipation.

use: The event takes ni: 'Nomikai ni sanka suru?' (Coming to the drinks?).

example.ja: 来週のパーティー、参加する？
example.english: Are you coming to next week's party?

examplePolite.romaji: Raishuu no paatii ni sanka shimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 来週のパーティーに参加しますか？
examplePolite.english: Will you be joining next week's party?

notes: A bit formal; between friends, iku (go) often does the job.

use: For loud partying or a big fuss: 'Sawaganaide' (Keep it down / Don't make a fuss).

example.romaji: Kinjo meiwaku da kara, sonna ni sawaganaide.
example.ja: 近所迷惑だから、そんなに騒がないで。
example.english: Don't make so much noise, you'll bother the neighbours.

examplePolite.romaji: Kinjo meiwaku desu kara, sawaganaide kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 近所迷惑ですから、騒がないでください。
examplePolite.english: Please keep the noise down for the neighbours.

notes: The noun sawagi means a commotion or uproar.

use: For looks or behaviour that catches the eye.

example.romaji: Sono akai fuku, sugoku medatsu ne.
example.ja: その赤い服、すごく目立つね。
example.english: That red outfit really stands out.

examplePolite.romaji: Sono akai fuku, sugoku medachimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: その赤い服、すごく目立ちますね。
examplePolite.english: That red outfit really stands out.

notes: Medachitagari is a show-off who wants attention.

english: break up (a group); call it a day
use: Said at the end of a gathering, often alone: 'Jaa, kaisan!' (OK, everyone can head home). Also a band splitting up.

example.romaji: Jaa, kyou wa kore de kaisan shiyou.
example.ja: じゃあ、今日はこれで解散しよう。
example.english: OK, let's call it a day here.

examplePolite.romaji: Dewa, kyou wa kore de kaisan shimashou.
examplePolite.ja: では、今日はこれで解散しましょう。
examplePolite.english: Well, let's call it a day here.

notes: For a couple breaking up, use wakareru, not kaisan.

use: After a verb stem it means 'keep on': 'tabetsuzukeru' (keep eating).

example.romaji: Mainichi tsuzukeru no ga taihen da yo.
example.ja: 毎日続けるのが大変だよ。
example.english: The hard part is keeping it up every day.

examplePolite.romaji: Mainichi tsuzukeru no ga taihen desu.
examplePolite.ja: 毎日続けるのが大変です。
examplePolite.english: The hard part is keeping it up every day.

notes: Tsuzuku is the version with no object: 'Ame ga tsuzuku' (The rain keeps going).

english: get tired of, get bored of
use: Usually in the past: 'Kono geemu, mou akita' (I'm bored of this game now). The thing takes ni.

example.romaji: Mainichi onaji gohan de, mou akita yo.
example.ja: 毎日同じご飯で、もう飽きたよ。
example.english: It's the same food every day, I'm sick of it.

examplePolite.romaji: Mainichi onaji gohan de, mou akimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 毎日同じご飯で、もう飽きました。
examplePolite.english: It's the same food every day, I'm tired of it.

notes: Not physically tired; that's tsukareru. Akippoi describes someone who gets bored quickly.

use: Usually pride in details; the thing takes ni.

example.romaji: Kare, koohii ni wa sugoku kodawaru n da yo.
example.ja: 彼、コーヒーにはすごくこだわるんだよ。
example.english: He's really particular about his coffee.

examplePolite.romaji: Kare wa koohii ni sugoku kodawaru n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 彼はコーヒーにすごくこだわるんですよ。
examplePolite.english: He's really particular about his coffee.

notes: The noun kodawari is a personal standard. It can also mean being hung up on something: 'Sonna koto ni kodawaranaide'.

english: reflect on one's mistakes, be sorry
use: For owning a mistake and resolving not to repeat it.

example.romaji: Kinou no koto, chanto hansei shiteru yo.
example.ja: 昨日のこと、ちゃんと反省してるよ。
example.english: I really am sorry about yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: Kinou no koto wa, hontou ni hansei shite imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日のことは、本当に反省しています。
examplePolite.english: I truly regret what happened yesterday.

notes: Stronger than a quick sorry. A hanseikai is a meeting to review what went wrong.

use: For things, people and health: 'Karada o daiji ni shite' (Look after yourself).

examplePolite.romaji: Okarada o daiji ni shite kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: お体を大事にしてくださいね。

notes: 'Odaiji ni' is the set phrase to someone who is ill: 'Get well soon'.

use: For people, gifts and memories you hold dear.

example.romaji: Kono purezento, zutto taisetsu ni suru ne.
example.ja: このプレゼント、ずっと大切にするね。

examplePolite.romaji: Kono purezento, zutto taisetsu ni shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: このプレゼント、ずっと大切にします。

notes: Nearly the same as daiji ni suru; taisetsu sounds a little warmer.

use: For kids, pets, juniors or ageing parents; the o is often dropped in speech.

example.romaji: Shuumatsu, inu no mendou mite kureru?
example.ja: 週末、犬の面倒見てくれる？
example.english: Can you look after my dog this weekend?

examplePolite.romaji: Shuumatsu, inu no mendou o mite itadakemasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: 週末、犬の面倒を見ていただけませんか？
examplePolite.english: Could you look after my dog this weekend?

notes: Mendou alone usually means a hassle, as in mendoukusai. 'Mendoumi ga ii' describes someone who looks out for others.

english: be looked after (by someone); owe someone
use: Mostly as thanks, 'Osewa ni narimashita', when leaving a job, a host or a hospital.

example.romaji: Iroiro sewa ni natta ne, arigatou.
example.ja: いろいろ世話になったね、ありがとう。
example.english: Thanks for everything you've done for me.

examplePolite.romaji: Iroiro osewa ni narimashita. Arigatou gozaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: いろいろお世話になりました。ありがとうございました。
examplePolite.english: Thank you for everything you've done for me.

notes: 'Osewa ni natte orimasu' opens work calls and emails, roughly 'Thanks for your continued support'.
